answers.answer: Verdicts: (a) DECEASED mid-century local icon = HARD NO. Cal. Civ. Code 3344.1 makes the right of publicity descendible for 70 years post-mortem, estate-enforced [FACT — kb3 POSTMORTEM_3344_1]; a decades-dead icon is still inside the window, plus any estate-held Class-25 mark. My spec: boundaries[4] 'the 70-year post-mortem right close[s] the ... dead-celebrity loophole.' (b) CURRENT CSU Stanislaus athlete under NIL = HARD NO. NIL lets even a local college athlete license and enforce their name, so 'just a local kid' is not a margin of safety [kb3 NIL_LOOPHOLE_CLOSE]; my boundaries[4] 'NIL ... close[s] the local-kid ... loophole.' The law that bites: Cal. Civ. 3344 (living right of publicity, fee-shifting) + potentially Lanham 43(a) false endorsement. (c) 2026 meme as a cleared LIMITED-DROP name = the ONE permitted carve-out, conditionally. glossary[drop-name carve-out] + boundaries[4]: 'cleared non-identity references allowed only as drop names.' The carve-out holds ONLY if the meme is (i) non-identity (references no real person/team/league/event tied to a real identity), (ii) cleared (no one owns the mark, trademark/transience checked), and (iii) quarantined to a drop, never the house brand. A meme that encodes a real person's identity is NOT carved out — it falls back to the four-law hard-no. So (c) is the single carve-out; (a) and (b) are hard-nos.
